findings.title: Git log record separator injection bypasses creditlint policy enforcement
findings.attack_path:
Attacker: any contributor who can open a pull request against a repository that runs creditlint in CI (the primary deployment model documented in README.md). Controlled input: the commit message body of their own commits. Path to vulnerable code: CI runs `creditlint check --range origin/main..HEAD` (or `creditlint audit --all`), which calls collect_range_messages/collect_all_messages in src/git.rs. Those functions invoke `git log --format=%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%cn%x1f%ce%x1f%B%x1e` and parse the output in parse_git_log_stream by splitting on the ASCII Record Separator (\x1e, U+001E) and Field Separator (\x1f, U+001F). Git preserves arbitrary control characters (including \x1e and \x1f) inside commit message bodies; only NUL (\x00) is forbidden. The attacker crafts a commit message such as `clean subject

body\x1eCo-authored-by: Codex <codex@example.com>
`. The injected \x1e inside %B causes parse_git_log_stream to split the single logical commit into two chunks. The first chunk's message field is truncated to the text before the injected separator (e.g. "body"). The text after the separator ("Co-authored-by: Codex <codex@example.com>") becomes a second chunk that parse_git_log_records attempts to parse as a new commit record, but it contains no \x1f field separators, so splitn(6, \x1f) yields only one field; the subsequent `fields.next()?` calls return None and filter_map silently discards the chunk. The violating trailer never reaches Policy::analyze. Verified end-to-end: a commit containing `Co-authored-by: Codex` hidden behind \x1e produces creditlint JSON output {"ok":true,"violations":[]} with exit code 0, while the identical commit without \x1e is correctly flagged with exit code 1. The same technique hides any forbidden freeform marker (e.g. `Made with Cursor`, `Generated with Claude`) and any forbidden trailer. The --message-file and --stdin paths are NOT affected because they feed text directly to Policy::analyze without the separator-based parser; only --range and audit --all (the CI/audit modes) are vulnerable.
findings.impact: A PR contributor can hide any forbidden authorship/credit marker (Co-authored-by trailers, Made-with/Generated-with markers, Author: identity lines) inside their commit messages so that creditlint's automated CI check reports zero violations and exits 0. The violating marker is still present in the git commit object and will land permanently in project history once the PR is merged, but creditlint -- the tool whose sole purpose is to block such markers before they land -- fails to detect it. On repositories where creditlint is a required CI check or is used for auto-merge gating, this allows AI/tool authorship markers to be silently introduced into protected branch history, defeating the project's stated enforcement model. The injected \x1e is a non-printable control character that renders as nothing or an inconspicuous symbol in most git log UIs and GitHub diffs, so human review provides weak detection.
findings.remediation: Use a record/field separator that cannot appear in git commit data. Git commit objects cannot contain NUL (\x00) bytes, so switch the --format string to use %x00 for both record and field separation (e.g. %H%x00%an%x00%ae%x00%cn%x00%ce%x00%B%x00) and parse with split on b'\x00'. Alternatively, invoke `git log -z` for NUL-terminated records. As defense-in-depth, validate that the first field of every parsed record matches a real git SHA (40-char hex / SHA-2) before accepting it, so injected fake records are rejected rather than silently dropped. Do not rely on \x1e/\x1f (or any printable-or-control byte other than NUL) as a separator for attacker-controlled git metadata.
